title: VPC peering (transitive routing limits)
hook: VPC peering connects two Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) at Layer 3 so private IP addresses can talk directly. It is not transitive: if VPC A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B.

blocks.text: A VPC peering connection links two VPCs so instances with private IPs can communicate as if on one extended network. AWS handles the backbone; you manage route tables, security groups, and Network Access Control Lists (NACLs). Peering works cross-account and cross-Region (with DNS considerations).

entries.plainDefinition: Bidirectional Layer 3 link between exactly two VPCs.
Peered VPCs do not advertise each other's routes to third VPCs.
entries.example: A↔B and B↔C does not give A↔C.

entries.plainDefinition: Peering requires distinct, non-overlapping IPv4/IPv6 ranges.

blocks.text: Peering is the simplest private link between two VPCs — shared services, tooling, or legacy split stacks. Interviewers test whether you know when peering breaks down (many VPCs, transitive needs, overlapping CIDR from acquisitions).

blocks.title: Scale limit
blocks.body: Full mesh peering among N VPCs needs N*(N-1)/2 connections — Transit Gateway replaces this pattern.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Create request
items.body: Requester specifies peer VPC ID and account if cross-account.

items.title: Add routes
items.body: Each side adds routes to peer CIDR (or specific subnets) pointing to pcx- id.

items.title: Open SG/NACL
items.body: Allow traffic on both sides — peering only provides reachability, not permission.

snippet.label: CLI — create peering
snippet.code:
aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection \
  --vpc-id vpc-requester \
  --peer-vpc-id vpc-accepter \
  --peer-region us-east-1
snippet.explanation: Cross-Region peering requires peer-region. Accepter must accept separately.

snippet.label: CLI — accept and route
snippet.code:
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-abc
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-a --destination-cidr-block 10.2.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id pcx-abc
snippet.explanation: Routes are per route table. Both directions need explicit routes for two-way traffic.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — peering + routes
snippet.code:
Peering:
  Type: AWS::EC2::VPCPeeringConnection
  Properties:
    VpcId: !Ref VpcA
    PeerVpcId: !Ref VpcB
RouteToB:
  Type: AWS::EC2::Route
  Properties:
    RouteTableId: !Ref VpcARouteTable
    DestinationCidrBlock: 10.2.0.0/16
    VpcPeeringConnectionId: !Ref Peering
snippet.explanation: CloudFormation cannot accept cross-account peering in one stack — often split stacks or custom resource.

snippet.label: CLI — verify peering options
snippet.explanation: Confirm active status and CIDR blocks before debugging SG rules.

blocks.title: Private connectivity mental model
rows: HTTP/gRPC between private IPs or DNS names
Service mesh may route through sidecars — different layer
Consul/Eureka or hard-coded internal ALB DNS

blocks.title: Pitfalls
blocks.body: Hub VPC pattern expecting transitive routes. Missing accepter routes. Referencing peer SG without enabling cross-VPC SG reference.

blocks.text: Peering is non-transitive by design — AWS avoids becoming your dynamic routing protocol. Cross-Region peering adds latency and separate DNS resolution options (enableDnsHostnames/enableDnsSupport on both). How to prove it in production: traceroute shows pcx hop; Flow Logs confirm SYN without reply implicates missing return route or SG.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Claiming peering is transitive through a shared VPC. Strong: only direct peer CIDRs route; third VPC needs its own peering or TGW attachment.

interviewTakeaways: VPC peering is one-to-one, non-transitive, and requires non-overlapping CIDR blocks.
Routes must exist on both sides; security groups can reference peer VPC groups in same Region/account.
Use Transit Gateway when you need hub-and-spoke beyond two VPCs — peering does not scale.
60s: Peering = private L3 between two VPCs. Not transitive. No overlapping CIDR. Update route tables both ways. SG rules still required. For many VPCs use TGW.
Follow-up: can you peer VPCs in different Regions and how does DNS resolution work?
commonPitfalls: Expecting transitive routing through a hub VPC gets you rejected — peering is always pairwise.
Strong answer: each peering is its own edge; routes are explicit per connection; use TGW for transitive hub.
Overlapping CIDR blocks — peering request fails or routing blackholes.
Forgetting return routes on the accepter side — asymmetric routing drops replies.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node services call peer VPC IPs via private DNS or ALB — peering is invisible at HTTP layer but required for packets to flow.
Typed clients targeting internal ALBs still need route tables and SG rules on both sides of the peering connection.
